SATURDAY. JANUARY 3, 1880.
FACTS FROM THE FINANCIAL REFORM
ALMANAC.

The IMencial Reform Altmme any be rmleed amongat the literary wonelere of .e age. Its pro- digious array of fact. and gores on matters political, social, and military, renders it Re a book of reference the mat oeofsl and valuable annual published. We had almoet eausidered that its elaborately tabulated atati.• Una information had year. ago reached to each a degree of excellence that there was wane ;mem for improvement, but it seems that this was not so, RN the admirable awe of the percent year wedeln, many valuable additiona. The Alogimac is more also than • valuable array or facts and figures, not the least entertaining and in- structive portion of the work being the slaewil and cleverly-written deductions of the editor There is material here for any amount of public apeaking and writing, cod it is a book that every voter ought to make himself aoquainted with before he goes to the ballot box at the next general election. We notice that the list of land holders of tea thomand scree and upwards published iu the Alamo. for 1879 has been this year extended en as to include holders of between 3,G00 and to,oto acres. This return, the editor observes, show. that 2,113 persons have upwards of 38,000,1530 SW., 11.11 d an estimated rental of £25,031,393, which, wadding to the apparent average rate on whieh these lands are let, muot be eery much below the real -mount. The mealy/de of the present House of Cmmuone brings out some curious facts. At the Cunureative geOliup or 0074, and proviona to the recent election fur the County Donegal, the Govern- ment maj wily was el. Aooording to the Xmas.. the majority is made up in this way The English constituencies return 073 Liberals and 283 Conserve- tivm ; the Welsh, 21 Liberals and 9 Conservatives ; the Scotch, 42 Liberals and to Coneervativea; and the Irish, 64 Liberals and 39 Conservative,. That it will be men that a Conservative Government could never hare been returned, and would, in fact, toe an in, possibility wereanot for the preponderating inflow.° of the English couutieti alone: and the influence of the Engliall counties is the influence of the landowners. The dheieeess editor seep that an examination of his figures will chow that the strength of the Conserva- tives lice in the English coludies, which, while the franchise am confined to freeholder., constituted the stronghold of their opponent. T. the :is., enfran- chisement of tenants at will—though for tho moot part these ate but the serfe of their landlords in polities— nod to the manipulation of the twenties in the Conservative Reform Bill of 1967, to emit Conoerva- tive purposes, the change is no doubt chiefly attribut- able. There in no just reaaon for maintaining the distinction between counties or boroughs, ea if these interests, rightly considered, were cot one and the same. THE TAY BRIDGE TRAGEDY.

,tn our last week'e issue we referred to the old year as. ! year of many unpleasant events, but correct more terrible than anything that had yet happened had still to come. The catastrophe which destroyed the train on the Tay bridge, on Sonde] night, included almost every element of horror. The train was crowded with a numerous and varied, and no doubt a joyoue company. 'There were ...Yen carriages all tined with passengers, old and young, etrong men in the prime of life women and little children, and all as helpless in the presence of this particular danger an babies in arms. The first accounts of the aceident.ccntsined on exaggerated estimate of the number of passengers, but the latest accounts ebow that there most have been in the train at level 90persous of all ages. An immense number of people surely to Ise hurled without almost 4 moment's warning to their death! Never has there been a calamity where the destruction was more sudden or unexpected, and yet, sudden ite it was, poa- sihlyilot eudden enough to exclude from the destroyed one dreadful moment of terrible agony. There wan no chance of escape fur anyone, no opportunity for the strongeet and moat active of the victims to make even an effort to escape destruction. The wind evrooped upon the bridge with a ' noise that is described as resembling a clap of thunder, and if amid the darkness and the gla.to when the first grinding crash came there rows from sat to sky one last farewell," it could not be heart above the roar of the elements by the few who witnessed the accident, which combine. within itself the horrors of shipwreck with those of a violent railway collision. It would not be easy to re- call an instance where the destruction was so complete end overwhelming as it was in this instance. And then the time of the year and the expected little family gatherings and festivities that no doubt caused so many passengers to be travelling by this feted train—are not these allition.,l B.fc,mstances of pain!

So great have been the engineering triumphs of the preeent century,-and to complete the victories which our engineers have obtained over natural obstructions and forces, that when a great work like the Tay Bridge is once completed and tested it is regardnl as rank heresy to doubt for • moment that it is note. safe and durable as the solid earth. It must have been so In this inamoce er neither railway officials or passenger. would have consented to the crossing of a heavily loaded train in the nntlat of what it now appears wall a terrible hurricane. On Sunday evening the wind ma. eweeping across the l'ay at the rate of 75 miles an hour, some of the more violent blasts attaining, it is said, a velocity of 90 miles. While the gale was at its height the team, with its living freight, ap- proached the bridge, and proceeded to cross at the usual slow pace of three miles an hour. It pasaed the signal box, entered man the bridge, and was seen no more. Ere the engine had cleared the central span, the bridge was struck by a terrific blast, and for a distauce of nearly half a mile it succumbsd to the tremendnua lateral preesure. Whether or not it would have done so if no train hail been on it at the time teat lean a debatable question that will never he satisfactorily decided. The engineers appear to he exercising their ingenuity to make it out that the train woe the cause of the accident, one of their theories being that some of the carriages first left the rails, and that the increased vibration which they occasioned broke the bridge. Another is that the premiere of the wind on the great girder* was very mall increased by the passing train cloeing the laticea, as it were, at a critical moment. But the popular, and In all likelihood the true opinion will be that, notwithstanding its splendid proportions, and the excellent Itutlity of the umterial, and the gill with which it eras rais,d, the engineers of the Tay Bridge mixalculated I the treinendons ferce of the tempeste to which it would he likely from time to time to be eapneed, and that sooner or later it must have yielded. The great and terrible misfortune is that a train laden with passengers should ham been pasaing at a moment when the bridge was being subjected to a lateral pressure of incalculable form.

And after all when everything is done that can he done we shall stiff have great catastrophies. There haVe been accidents always, and the only difference. that now-adays we are liable to encounter them on a gigantic 6.1 e. We meve about in trains containing hundreds and even thou- sand. of our fellow being, through tunnels and over bridges and viaducts that our ancestors knew nothing of, and that while they give new facilities for comfortable and speedy travelling call freuh perils into being. Engineering skill may reduce the chances of accident to a minimum but they cannot ensure absolute eatery. In vain may we build our splendid and powerful steam vessels, in vain may our fleets sweep over the stormiest of N.., in vain trains may run their journeys for years without mishap, there will be terrible shipwrecks net low of life at sea and catastrophies on land to the end of the chai-ter. In former days it was a nuil coach that was upset and a few people killed or maimed, now it is an express train and COMee to grief, and the loss of life W appalling. The circumstances are different, but we must gill confess that, whether on land or sea, .atastropldes enter int-, the mysterious scheme of that's providence. And not only so, hot when they do occur all seem to suffer alike, the good and the bad, the strong and the weak, the old and wayworn, and the innocent child, brimful of life and anhnsl spirits, all are slain with • like Violence, without werning, arid apparently without metcy.

intended asking through your paper whether the Liberals of St. Helens were going to be ovt reseed and • plietened by the Toryisms of Colonel .1. Ireland Blackburne, who gave us a pr. e of his oratory .t week or two Anne in the Town Hall. I see, Imwever, that our friends are not altogether dead, as Mr. Noble, of London, is announced to give us a lecture, under the auspices of the St. Helene Liberal Association. on "11,0 luxuries ol a Conservative Government." Mr. Noble has been several Ames iv hiS I diarict, aid is getting very popular. We have had already the upholder of" constitutional usag,v " giving or his view. Ind defending the Governtnent from the "groan attacks " rude upon it, and the " cruel reports " which have been circulated about it and, I think, not too largely circulated. Gruel reporta, indeed I have been told by persons of age alltk experience th.tt prosperity and a Tory Government never had acy affinity for each other, coil believe it but what puzzles me most. is a wooing man being • Conservative. And there are few of thew in St. I lelene, or of those who profess to be. We have "political parsons" in St. Helens who are not ashamed of showing their colour, and we have also those who profesa to : be' nothing," or " neutral." but who are thorough Tories to the backlone. If tele had parsons who would talk to people we umdar subjects as well as sacred, I believe that we should have a dwindling down of Conservative working men. Working men of St. Helens, secure a ticket for the leeture on Monday night, and hear robot the "luxuries of a Conserva- tive Government" are, and if you are Comervatives on Tart- day morning you astonish A YOUNG LIBERAL WORKING MAN. die—it is often said we live in a wonderful age. Very often things are weighed against gold. How much will it being. brood more frequently than how much good will it bring ? Ilutlsham is a wonderful village. Last week the parishioners attended a meeting, which certainly passed east resolutions, but about what I could not learn. 'Phis week we have had another meeting to rouse the people from :hair apathy. A few years since, we recollect well, a poor man uwal hi go along the wide street wiling sand, with a donkey •nd cart, named Billy or William Tweedale. Thie poor fellow once thought he could improve his circum- stances Loy securing a broken-down horse to drag the cart. ee ho, went to a retired schoolmaster, Mr. Rowe, thew living in Alvauley village,and stated his errand. To out the story short, poor Billv obtained more pounds from those charitably disposed, although he never • obtained the pony. This IA Will the case in the annals of . Fraishsni. The former iso case worthy of ampot. and ought to be suprarted by everybody, and they I go P. work it, A straightforward wee, but the Free Chutch, a Methodist place ot worship, with Probably not more than a down members, are determined to build a manse. This is a laudable object, no doubt. but to attain their object they spen a bazaar, held last Tuesday, mid resort to pushing practices to rt rid or the goods. Thu., one Young lade with =therm, of been exhorted the ember-minded to buy her bean-pie. Lucky bags were also in vogue, although this created an un- eeemly tumult and confusion. Now, gambling. or rather to see the refined word. raffling, was, Mr. Editor. at the very taut, unbecoming in such a piece. No one more strongly than Spurgeon bee condemned bazaars for religious pur- paws. and why ? Solely because of the tendency of this raffling. Suppose I was a family man instead or being a bachelor, should I like my children, after doing ell I could to inatil moral truths into their minds, to be led antral hy thie very raffling? Does it not lead to playing for money, and by gradual steps lead to gambling? Sooner the various religious organizations in the country see this tendency the better. Nay, it would be better to discard them fancy sales and Chrietmas trees altogether, and instead honestly appeal to the people or help. If the ia good, no one need fear denial. Just fancy raffling a large rake, then a cushmn, afterwards to come to • doll. By chic time oil the young people are full of excitement you may fomtell, without laying claim to be a seer, the evil efforts of this whirl of excitement. Am I wrong in stating that all the fruit of the previous Sabbath's teaching, both from wbool and pnlpit, is hat purely from this want of thought' The village is in a abocaing condition. A few years ego seldom • week pawed ' away but we had a temperance meeting, reaulting in the olosing of three beethouses. div.p: RUNCORN PARISH CHURCH TEA PARTY.

SPEECHES BY THE HON V "EGERTON, M.P., AND HR. P. EGERTON WARBURTON, M.P. Last night the congregational tea party in co„„,,Kino with the Runcorn Parish Church, was held in the National Infants' Schoolroom. The Any. Canon Barclay, the vicar, presided at the meeting which afterwards took place and which was crowded No doubt the very large attendance might he i aome measure accounted for owing to the presence of the two inernbors for Mid-Cheshire— the 1n,,. Wilbraham Eg,ton, Ml'., and Mr. Piers Egerton Warburton, I'. Amongnt tho,e present were the Revs. W. Preson, A. Ford, J. J. Bryant, W. Robinson, It B. Blogg, Mr. icorge Garrett, Mr. Whittaker, Mr. Briscoe, Mr. I.yurt. Mr. Guinn, Mr. John Ashton, and Mr. Robert Aehlon. .

The Citatulag, in ,pening the proceedings, said he bad the double duty to perform it the tatne of the nisi.] gueste—an I those includest all th.e who had worked for them dering the past year in connection with the church and he Legge!: to thank the other metsibers of the compeo- tion for their courtesr in giving them such a genial invitation, :not to thank those who were clmrch-workers far It tying no cordially responded to the invitation and come mond in each force that night. Them had nothing occurred during the past year, on which he needed dwell more especially as binational letter which contained a report of the parochial institutiont wat published late this year in order to bring in the account of Hach. schools. The schools were a very no part of their parochial machinery, and fur that reason the ann.l let., was delayed. There was one into he always performed on that occasion and it very pleasant duty it was. and that was to notice the services of their church officiate, and they ;nest pardon him for inoment while be alluded to those who had been amongst them in that otj.aaity for many years, and who were not resent that evening. li, might allude tirat to Mr. Hartley who for 17 mars—first :is parish clerk and then vicar's cAltl,llWArtlell--CODUiblltfil all his energies, his professional energies .nal eapecial seal in order to render the services of the church wurthy of the building in which they were per- formed, and worthy of llirn in whose behalf they Vele per- formed. Ni.d exactly sicknees but lameness had prevented hint to the last few years of his office attending to the church set% ices, and he felt P hie conscientiooe duty to resign in pl.we of those who °mild do the work. Hewes owe all of them mere ready to acknowledge the valuable services be had renole,sl thetn during the 118{ IT years. (Applause.) Unonno,coo any 000 01 their officials, who rendered in hie time tel service to the church, and who Imd his hand M his nott for every Omen of charity whatever W. the position or aet of the party applying, had been taken sway front them. Mr. ChM. Christopher 'union they were aware God hut called to his rest during the past year, and they could but regret the loss of those who had worked with them in time. past. Referring to the churchwardens and sideemen, he said he thought lie was justified in aayllag them could not he fond four such tnen in any parish— . epplausel—and he simply asked them to respond with a round of applause in the.shape of a vote of thanks folk. churchwardens and two sidesmen for their efficient servietli. Loud applause.) A song and quartet having been given,

'Fbe (Test wsw mid that for the last seven or eight ymrs be had been connected with the Hon. Wilbraham Egerton in connection with the Diocesan Chaities, A Ild they all of them had reason to he thankful for the good advice Ito gave them-0w good, practical relvice—on all occseions, and es- pecially for the help in organising the varioth institution, which be (the chairman) had the honour of bringing before Hole notice some time ago, and he thought to himself that as that was the congregational tea party connected with the Fari,h Church, be might fairly appeal to Mr. Egerton. as the chairman, to put in an appearance, and help him at that thnual soiree. /le kindly responded to the invitation, and he now had the pleasure of calling upon him to propose the next vote of thanks (Applanse.) Hon. WI I.PRANVI EOII2TON then rose and ~aid . Canon Betclay, Imlies and gentlemen,—l have responded to the invitation—the very friendly invitation—of Canon Bereith to be present here this evening. My acquaintance with him does not date hick to the seven or eight years hut to a Yen much longer time, and I well remember the kindness with which he at in my other places has welcomed one. When I came to Rancor, mme than 20 years ago, to cane-em as your repreentativ, I well remember the kindness of one tliat has gone from as now—Mr. Whiteway—and many other members of his family thereto e, I can say uow my monection in Runcorn datm for over 200 roars. vero glad to be present on this ocm•ion and see the work which Can. Barclay is doing for Runcorn, and if I man to anything in the way of awisting him with his work and testify on sympathy by my preeence of anything I can say en the occaelon Ilehould only be too !many. (Applause.) I have been asked to move a vete of thanks, and I am reminded by the preeence of ladies that this in a mein!, and not a politimil meeting thereto, as to the remarks I bare to Athena to you, they will be directed rather to the poeition of church mark and church workers at the present time. We are all, I suppose, here supporters of the Church of England , and I venture to think that it will b. an evil dey for this mutiny if ever there are wanting supporters of it, for it Pr one of the oldeet institutions in this cOuntry, and has grown up with and contributed so largely to thr welfare of thie country (Applause.) And among its ehiefest merits are those imtit Miens, parochial organisations, the remit of which we see here to-day. It is extended over the length thd breadth of the land, and it brings home tri everyone its spiritml ministration. and blessinth-of Goepel truth to all, which is given freely to all without restriction either of creed or of position in life. The Church of England is the meet comprehensive of all religious institutions of tide country , for everyone, by hie birth neon Englishman, is a member of our national Church. Well, think, sir, we should remember the pr:vilegee tbat we have, and avail ourselves of it ae niuch as we can, and endeavour, by showing s goal example to others., to enlist the sympathies of all in carrying ! out the great work of the Chiral of Ertgland, which is spreading a knowleige of tooth among the whole of the people, and assisting the Government of the country by teaching every aystem of morality which is hointled, not an heathen philosophy. but on the doctrines of the Gospel. (Applause.) In other countries there may In different . systems. It is not a queetion with us whether, in point of theory, the national Church is a good thing or not, as it may be in 1110 case of a new COlll., like Aintrim ; but we ! have hot a systematical exposition of the doctrines of the Church of England for many years. It is a precious hen. tags which has been handed down to us by our forefathers, and we should do everything we can to hand it down to our children pure and unsullied. The object of meeting, sir, is thin, as I understand—to rally round the entre, the vicar of the parish—to rally round him all the workers who carry oat his wwk end support hint during the ymr. t Bu the Church of England does not conline itself to those who take enders, but largely encourages, nth is glad to mail itself of. the services of laymen 0 end it is to them that lock you to marry the vote of thanks this evening. There are numerous charitim awl institutions in connection with the onpinisetions of the parish. You have a fund for adding to the sdariesof curatmand tam sure if we consider the very small salaries which many of the clergy of the Church of EnglanJ are content to live on Sum sure that every exertion that you can make to give theman adequate salary is one deserving of your support. (Applause.) When we look at the number who are content, in the high muse in which they are engaged, with • , salery which ie very often not more than that of a skilled ! workman, if even so much as that of a skilled workmao, who give up their whole lives to the good work ie which they arc ! engaged, it is quite clear that it is oat thy ternmation of the eatery but the wish to do a good work among you that en- ables them to remain on so little. Then again there is a most admirable institution I see here—the penny bank. Now, perhaps the English people artrk harder than thy other people in the world, but I am afraid they do not always save up en much as other countries what they mm, therefore any encouragement as of that llnd—same ee the penny oank—ie one which ought to be encourage/ among at. If we could ouly get the working class to pot, by one-half or the greater part of what is spent in drink, we ; should be entirely independent of the reverses in trade and bed tirnm—(applause)—becaune you would then have a store laid by to meet what is called ° the rainy day," or bad times, bemuse people are too apt to forget that prosperity comes in Imps and bounds. But as you cannot expect to have a con- tinuo. awl united time of prosperity, every man, whatever his iosition in life may be, is hound to make provision for reverties. Such is the admirable eystem of insurance, the penny bank is, to a certain extent, to the workman an insurance againet sickness, had times, short lahour, and of lovt wages. If the Frond, pesple had been a very much more forgot and saving people than we arethey would not have been able to pay off the enormous debt which they incurred in their war with Germany. But Duch are the caving qualities of the French people that about eight or nine years after their having paid that enormous sum to the Germans, they Oct trow a wealthier people titan the Germans to whom they paid those hundreds of millions. Therefore that is one of tl• advantages of the peony tank. It teaches the people of this country, the working classes—it teaches them the admen sages of teeing. and ones them the opportunity of putting by toe rainy day. The next thing I see is the National Schools are among your parochial organisations Well, we ell know in these drys how soon schools have been extended among lie, and I ant glad to hear that for the most part the schools here are entirely eupported by the voluntary effort at by denominations, and althonah you have • School Board there are or yet net Board schools among them. I always sympathise with those who endeavour to keep up denominational schools, for I believe that the leaching in thetu—although Board schools are admirable for secular education, yet by their constitution they mnnot teach such religious truth A 8 ought to be inculcated among the young in the same Iveyas could be taught in the (shard] aehools. (Applause.) But I most not detain you too long in speaking of the parochial organ.mtions. I can only say I trust that it will maintain its good effichncy during the 000, 04 poor; hut before I sit done I must wish You "A happy new year.' ands more prosperous one then the year 1870 I Now I believe at Ronan, that trade has not been so hot asat other places. I am glad to my that the salt trade during the preterit year has betel as goyd, if not better, than it has been for mme years, and I know how much the prosperity of itimmrn depend. upon the trade which is brought toy the Weaver and by the mnal. lam told also that the pottery trade his continued Sr flourish. in spite of tad tam 0, snd I ern not =misled at that, t.,000 herever you go abroad you will find that the adrnimble dmigns and the exc..llent texture of English etoneware and china meek With unlvemal approval; awl it is one of those thing. in which we have—after agraaldo.l of trouble, I believe—beaten the foreigner out of the fled to • very consklemble extent, and I trust we may long continue the- superi,wity in that it not in other brandies of toads. (Applause./ No doebt the tad trade we have hid has been occmionel he it variety of sourcea over many of which it is impossibl,l fee any one of as to have control. noon has bean, no doubt, over pro- duction, and there I, IS bleu a great deal of 00cr speculation conaccoana 01 mine ymrs. A great deal of mmer has been spent In t 0... ,fi moor wh.cii niOt n-v 4 r come tar), to the people of this country. Hat we have also Wel lb, had haraeata, and that mast hare had a very material effect upon the consumption of those articles otanu- facturel In this country. Daylight 4.1111 now td chowiati, cad than, maim to De a 'right

ray of eunshine beginning to pies over our trade. We truet that in the course of this veer the sun will again shine brilliantly upon our hade. Wo have had alm many calarititirs this last year, not to speak of the last great caland y, that dreadful accident to the Toy bridge, which has met •gloorn upon all of us at this time. We have had , rumour. of ware all over Europe. Happily anything like a Ettropean war, has, I believe, by the prudence of our (hymn- . 000,00 been averted. We hal, also had what was undoubtedly a great dimmer in Africa. —one of those case. which every nation tellable to—o eml. den and unforeseen disaster moo wikl and savage country. . That war was occasioned, is you know, by our having as a neighbour e reckless savage, whose cloief object in life was . said to be that his young moo should wash their spear. in . the blood of their neighbours. It was not, however, there- , foie to he surprised at that Hy colonista with such migh- t boatman these took the initiative. and endeaveurmi to bring matters to • crisis—whether rightly or wrongly I do not my I —but one is not altogether surptised that they I did do no, However, I hope in the future it • • may not occur again. Rut the war has happilYl been now closed, and we trust in South Africa we should not I have any recurrence of war or any olimster”uchas we have had during the past year. Hut although we have had dis- asters, yet many of them have been wiped out to a great ex- tent. Consequently the diamter of leandula hoe been wiped out by the glorious victory of Ulundi. 'Ohe name thing lone happenwl in the caw of the eastern war in Afghanietan. Well, at the beginning of this year n-e had a hollow peace made with the ruler of that country who, fro, mettle that have since happened, meet dently have been corrupted by Ruasian intrigue as far as we can see. Hut after that diagraceful and cowardly massacre of Sir Louis Cavagnari we have indicted a severe end deeervert punishment upon those wild Afghan tribes, and now inst..] of our gallant troop in Cabal having to eat their Christmas dinner with the fear of those thousands of Afghans coming down Limn them at any ante, we are happy, in the mws we have just received, to learn that by Christmas day they signally defeated and routed theta. Therefore in that direction also such a eanpltte victory givm on a proep.ct of secure and lasting peace in Coot somewhat turbalent country. Well, I ttliat that in the pre. cent year we may have better trade, peaceful relatiom with all the world, and last, but not least, we trust that Providence mav give thin awintry more sunny weather .tnd a good ha, vent. (Applause.) I feel certain that if the harvest proves to be a good one that will be one of the best and midiont onems of a recurrence of prosperity and improvement in out trade. I have now, I think, nothing more to add ; bet in wiahing you a very happy New Ymr, look you to agree with me in the vote of thanks to Mr. Brandi at for his aer. ViCeil 3s banterer of the Additional Cumtes' Fund, Penny Honk, and Newtown mission milord; and Mr. Whittaker, for hie services ex treaaurer of the Runcorn national schools. (Loud applame.) Mr. JON,. BRMUDItiT, who was received with chews, was called forward in order to reply to the vote of thanks. He said that for a full statement of facts in connection with their parochial work, ke would refer them both, letter issued by Canon Barclay sonie Hate during loot summer. In that document they would find ail matters connected with the church work put before them in a very exhaustive manner. He referred to the fact that the Additional Curetes' Smiety, of which Ire was treimurer, was in need of funds. They would see frotn the Canon's statement that the Penny Bank wan in on very flourishing condition. Of,.
